title: Measurement & Units
blurb: The metric ladders for length, mass and capacity, the base-sixty ladder of time, elapsed-time reckoning, and measurement problems solved convert-first.

lessons.title: Units of Length
lessons.concreteComparison: A pencil is $17$ cm, a ger is about $6$ m across, and the road from Ulaanbaatar to Darkhan runs $220$ km. Measuring the road in centimetres would take a $22$-million-count; measuring the pencil in kilometres would need a decimal with a parade of zeros. Units are TOOLS — you pick the one sized to the job, and convert when jobs meet.
lessons.objective: Know the metric length ladder (mm, cm, m, km), choose the sensible unit for a task, and convert in both directions — including mixed forms like 3 m 45 cm.
concept: **The length ladder.** $1$ cm $= 10$ mm; $1$ m $= 100$ cm; $1$ km $= 1\,000$ m. The rungs are place-value shifts — ×$10$, ×$100$, ×$1\,000$ — so converting is Topic 5's ladder-walking with unit names attached.
**Down the ladder multiplies.** A bigger unit re-counted in a smaller one needs MORE of them: $3$ m $= 300$ cm. Mixed forms unfold the same way: $3$ m $45$ cm $= 300 + 45 = 345$ cm.

**Up the ladder divides.** $2\,500$ m $= 2$ km $500$ m — or, with a decimal, $2.5$ km. Choosing the unit is part of the answer: a carpenter says $345$ cm, a mapmaker says $2.5$ km, and both are re-counting, not re-measuring.
lessons.keyIdea: A measurement is a count of units. Converting re-counts the same length: down the ladder multiplies (more, smaller units), up the ladder divides.

facts.title: The length ladder
facts.explanation: Three rungs, all powers of ten — the metric system's whole design.

facts.title: Mixed form unfolds
facts.explanation: Convert the big part, then add the small part — place value with names.

workedExamples.statement: A plank measures $3$ m $45$ cm. Express it in centimetres, and in metres as a decimal.
workedExamples.note: Unfold the metres; then rename with the decimal ladder.
workedExamples.solution: Centimetres: $3 \times 100 + 45 = 345$ cm. As metres: $345$ cm $= \frac{345}{100}$ m $= 3.45$ m — Topic 5's staircase wearing a unit.

workedExamples.statement: A trail is $2\,500$ m long. Write it in kilometres-and-metres, and as a decimal of kilometres.

commonMistakes.text: Converting metres to centimetres by ×10 — 3 m = 30 cm.
commonMistakes.correction: Each rung has its own factor: m→cm is ×100 (3 m = 300 cm); only cm→mm is ×10. Say the rung's factor before multiplying.

commonMistakes.text: Multiplying when going UP the ladder — 2,500 m = 2,500,000 km.
commonMistakes.correction: Bigger units mean FEWER of them: going up divides. 2,500 m ÷ 1,000 = 2.5 km. Sanity: a trail can't be two and a half million kilometres.

tryIt.statement: Convert $7$ m $8$ cm to centimetres. (Watch the missing tens.)
tryIt.solution: $7 \times 100 + 8 = 708$ cm — the zero tens hold their place, exactly as in Topic 1.

tryIt.statement: A ribbon is $460$ cm. Express it in metres-and-centimetres, and decide: is it longer than $4.5$ m?

steps.title: Pick the tool, know the ladder
beats: Millimetres for a coin's thickness, centimetres for a pencil, metres for a ger, kilometres for a road — units are tools sized to jobs.
The ladder: $1$ cm $= 10$ mm, $1$ m $= 100$ cm, $1$ km $= 1\,000$ m — every rung a power of ten.
DOWN the ladder multiplies: the same length re-counted in smaller units needs more of them. $3$ m $= 300$ cm; and $3$ m $45$ cm unfolds to $345$ cm.

steps.title: The metre lives in Paris
steps.body: For over a century the metre WAS a physical platinum bar kept in a Paris vault — every ruler on earth a copy of it. Today it's defined by the speed of light, so no fire or thief can change how long a metre is.

steps.title: Up the ladder, and mixed decisions
beats: UP the ladder divides — bigger units, fewer of them: $2\,500$ m $= 2.5$ km, or $2$ km $500$ m.
The decimals topic pays off here: $\div 1\,000$ walks the digits three steps — $460$ cm $= 4.6$ m.
Which form to use is a communication choice: the carpenter's $345$ cm, the runner's $2.5$ km — same lengths, different audiences.

steps.title: Up the ladder
steps.intro: Divide out the rung; the remainder keeps the small unit.

options: divide by $1\,000$ — bigger unit, fewer of them
steps.explanation: Up the ladder divides: $1\,200 \div 1\,000 = 1.2$ km. (Multiplying would claim the walk got a thousand times longer by renaming it.)

steps.title: What you learned
points: The ladder: 10 mm in a cm, 100 cm in a m, 1,000 m in a km.
Down the ladder multiplies; up the ladder divides — say the rung's factor first.

The decimal staircase does the up-conversions: 460 cm = 4.6 m.

steps.title: You've finished "Units of Length"
steps.body: One ladder, three rungs, two directions. Mass and capacity next — the same design with new names, which is exactly why the metric system conquered the world.

lessons.title: Mass & Capacity
lessons.concreteComparison: A packet of tea is $250$ g, a sack of flour $25$ kg, and a loaded truck $3$ tonnes. A cup of airag holds $250$ ml; the jug, $2$ litres. Mass and capacity run on the same ladder design as length — thousand-steps between neighbours — so everything you did with metres transfers in one move.
lessons.objective: Convert between grams, kilograms and tonnes, and between millilitres and litres, including mixed forms and how-many-fit problems.
concept: **The mass ladder.** $1$ kg $= 1\,000$ g; $1$ tonne $= 1\,000$ kg. Two rungs, both thousand-steps: $2$ kg $350$ g $= 2\,350$ g, and $4\,700$ kg $= 4$ t $700$ kg.
**The capacity ladder.** $1$ L $= 1\,000$ ml — one rung, same design: $1.5$ L $= 1\,500$ ml. (Capacity measures how much a container HOLDS; the units are litres and their thousandths.)
**How many fit?** Capacity problems love division: a $2$ L jug fills $2\,000 \div 250 = 8$ cups of $250$ ml. Convert to ONE unit first; then it's Topic 3's division, receipts and all.
lessons.keyIdea: Mass and capacity reuse the length ladder's design — thousand-steps between units. Convert to one unit, then count, add, or divide as usual.

facts.title: The mass ladder
facts.explanation: Two thousand-step rungs — grams to kilograms to tonnes.

facts.title: The capacity rung
facts.explanation: One rung; a millilitre is a thousandth of a litre.

workedExamples.statement: A parcel weighs $2$ kg $350$ g. Express it in grams, and as a decimal of kilograms.
workedExamples.note: Thousand-step down, then the staircase back up.

workedExamples.statement: How many $250$ ml cups does a $2$ L jug fill?
workedExamples.solution: Convert: $2$ L $= 2\,000$ ml. Divide: $2\,000 \div 250 = 8$ cups. Receipt: $8 \times 250 = 2\,000$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Converting kg to g by ×100 because metres did that.
commonMistakes.correction: The mass rungs are THOUSAND-steps: 1 kg = 1,000 g. Each ladder has its own factors — say the rung before you multiply.

commonMistakes.text: Dividing mixed units directly — "2 L ÷ 250 ml = 0.008".
commonMistakes.correction: Convert to ONE unit first: 2,000 ml ÷ 250 ml = 8 cups. Mixed-unit arithmetic is the cardinal sin of measurement.

steps.title: The thousand-step ladders
beats: Mass climbs by thousands: $1$ kg $= 1\,000$ g, $1$ tonne $= 1\,000$ kg. A tea packet is grams, a flour sack kilograms, a loaded truck tonnes.
Mixed forms unfold as with length: $2$ kg $350$ g $= 2\,350$ g; and the staircase renames upward: $2\,350$ g $= 2.35$ kg.
Same design as metres — only the factors changed. Say the rung ("kg to g, times a thousand") and the length habits transfer whole.

Which is HEAVIER: $0.8$ kg or $795$ g?
problems.explanation: One unit: $0.8$ kg $= 800$ g $> 795$ g — by five grams.

steps.title: Which unit?
steps.prompt: A sheep's mass is most sensibly given in:
steps.explanation: A sheep runs tens of kilograms — about $50$ kg. Grams would need $50\,000$; tonnes would need $0.05$; and millilitres measure liquid, not mass.

steps.title: A litre of water weighs a kilogram
steps.body: The metric system's secret handshake: $1$ litre of water has a mass of almost exactly $1$ kilogram — the units were DESIGNED to match. A $2$ L bottle of water: about $2$ kg. No other measurement system ever linked its ladders so neatly.

steps.title: Capacity, and how-many-fit
beats: Capacity — how much a container holds — runs one rung: $1$ L $= 1\,000$ ml. A cup is $250$ ml; a kettle, $1.7$ L.
How-many-fit questions are divisions in disguise: a $2$ L jug into $250$ ml cups — convert first ($2\,000$ ml), then divide: $8$ cups.
Leftovers behave like Topic 3: $1\,500 \div 200 = 7$ r $100$ — seven full glasses and $100$ ml left, receipt and all.

steps.title: Capacity work
steps.intro: One unit, then divide with receipts.

steps.title: The cardinal sin
steps.prompt: To find how many $250$ ml cups a $2$ L jug fills, a student computes $2 \div 250$. The fix:
steps.explanation: Litres and millilitres cannot meet in one division. Re-count the jug in millilitres ($2\,000$), THEN divide: $8$ cups.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Mass: 1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 t = 1,000 kg. Capacity: 1 L = 1,000 ml.
Same ladder design as length — only the factors differ; name the rung first.
How-many-fit = convert to one unit, then divide (receipts included).
Never compute across mixed units — the cardinal sin of measurement.

steps.title: You've finished "Mass & Capacity"
steps.body: Two more ladders, zero new ideas — the metric design pays its dividend. Next: TIME, the one ladder that refuses to run on tens.

lessons.title: Units of Time
lessons.concreteComparison: Every ladder so far ran on tens — and then comes the clock. Sixty seconds to a minute, sixty minutes to an hour, twenty-four hours to a day: time's ladder was built four thousand years ago in Babylon, long before decimals, and it never converted. One habit must change: with time you trade by SIXTIES, and the ×10 reflexes must stay at the door.
lessons.objective: Convert between seconds, minutes, hours and days — including mixed forms and fraction-of-an-hour amounts — without importing base-ten reflexes.
concept: **The sixty-ladder.** $1$ min $= 60$ s; $1$ h $= 60$ min; $1$ day $= 24$ h; $1$ week $= 7$ days. No tens anywhere — each rung has its own factor, and each must be said aloud.
**Mixed forms trade by the rung.** $2$ h $15$ min $= 2 \times 60 + 15 = 135$ min. Backwards: $200$ s $= 3$ min $20$ s, because $200 \div 60 = 3$ r $20$ — division with remainders, wearing a watch.

**Fractions of an hour are sixtieths.** Half an hour $= 30$ min; a quarter $= 15$; three-quarters $= 45$. The decimal trap: $1.5$ h $= 90$ min, NOT $150$ — the $0.5$ multiplies sixty, never a hundred.
lessons.keyIdea: Time trades by sixties (and twenty-fours), not tens: convert with the rung's own factor, use division with remainders for mixed forms, and never let 1.5 h become 150 minutes.

facts.title: The sixty-ladder
facts.explanation: Babylonian rungs — no tens; each factor said aloud.

facts.title: The decimal trap
facts.explanation: Half an hour is thirty minutes — the .5 multiplies sixty.

workedExamples.statement: Convert $2$ h $15$ min to minutes, and $200$ s to minutes-and-seconds.
workedExamples.note: Down: ×60 and add. Up: divide by 60, keep the remainder.
workedExamples.solution: Down: $2 \times 60 + 15 = 135$ min. Up: $200 \div 60 = 3$ r $20$ — three minutes twenty seconds. Receipt: $3 \times 60 + 20 = 200$ ✓.

workedExamples.statement: A film lasts $1.5$ hours. How many minutes is that — and why is $150$ wrong?
workedExamples.solution: $1.5$ h $= 1$ h $+ \frac{1}{2}$ h $= 60 + 30 = 90$ min. Writing $150$ applies the base-ten reflex ($1.5 \times 100$) to a base-sixty ladder — half an hour has thirty minutes, not fifty.

commonMistakes.text: Converting 1.5 h to 150 min — the ×100 reflex on a ×60 ladder.
commonMistakes.correction: The decimal part multiplies SIXTY: 0.5 × 60 = 30, so 1.5 h = 90 min. Time is the one ladder where decimal shifting lies.

commonMistakes.text: Writing 200 s as 2 min 00 s — dividing by 100.
commonMistakes.correction: Divide by 60: 200 = 3 × 60 + 20, so 3 min 20 s. The remainder must stay under 60 — a '2 min 80 s' answer stopped early.

tryIt.statement: Convert $3$ h $40$ min to minutes, and $500$ s to minutes-and-seconds.
How many minutes are in $\frac{3}{4}$ of an hour? In $2\frac{1}{4}$ hours?

steps.title: The ladder that refuses tens
beats: Time's rungs: $60$ s to the minute, $60$ min to the hour, $24$ h to the day, $7$ days to the week. Not a ten in sight.
Down the ladder still multiplies — by the RUNG'S factor: $2$ h $15$ min $= 2 \times 60 + 15 = 135$ min.
Up the ladder is division with remainders: $200$ s $= 3$ min $20$ s ($200 \div 60 = 3$ r $20$) — and the remainder must stay under sixty.

Convert $3$ days to hours, and $100$ h to days-and-hours.

steps.title: Rung by rung
steps.intro: Say the factor — 60 or 24 — before converting.

steps.title: Remainder discipline
steps.prompt: A student writes $170$ s $= 2$ min $50$ s. Verdict:
options: wrong — it should be $1$ min $70$ s
steps.explanation: Receipt: $120 + 50 = 170$ ✓, remainder under sixty ✓. ($1$ min $70$ s names the same amount but stopped trading early.)

steps.title: Blame Babylon
steps.body: Sixty survives from Babylonian astronomy: $60$ divides evenly by $2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20$ and $30$ — perfect for splitting hours into clean parts. A decimal clock was actually tried during the French Revolution ($10$-hour days!); it lasted about two years.

steps.title: Fractions of an hour, and the trap
beats: An hour splits like any whole: half $= 30$ min, a quarter $= 15$, three-quarters $= 45$ — the fraction multiplies SIXTY.
The decimal trap: $1.5$ h is $1$ h $+ 0.5 \times 60 = 90$ min. The $\times 100$ reflex says $150$ — and lies.
Mixed hours convert the same way: $2\frac{1}{4}$ h $= 120 + 15 = 135$ min. Fractions of a minute too: $\frac{1}{2}$ min $= 30$ s.

steps.title: Hour fractions
steps.intro: The fraction multiplies sixty, never a hundred.

examples.prompt: How many minutes in $1.5$ h?
steps: $90$ min — the $150$ answer used the wrong ladder.

$2.5$ h equals:
problems.explanation: $120 + 30 = 150$ min — and here $150$ IS right, because $2.5 \times 60 = 150$. (The trap is using $\times 100$; $2.5 \times 100$ would give $250$.)

steps.title: Spot the ladder
steps.explanation: $1.2$ h $= 60 + 0.2 \times 60 = 72$ min — the $120$ came from $\times 100$. The others all multiplied sixty honestly.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Time's rungs: 60 s, 60 min, 24 h, 7 days — no tens anywhere.
Down multiplies by the rung's factor; up divides with a remainder under it.
Fractions of an hour multiply sixty: 3/4 h = 45 min.
The decimal trap: 1.5 h = 90 min — the ×100 reflex lies on this ladder.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before every conversion say WHICH sixty (or twenty-four) you're trading — the spoken factor is the whole defence.

problems.explanation: A quarter of sixty: $15$ min. ($25$ is the decimal-digits reflex again.)

steps.title: You've finished "Units of Time"
steps.body: The one ladder that trades by sixties — and now its traps are labelled. Next: reading the clock in motion, where counting up through round hours does all the work.

lessons.title: Elapsed Time
lessons.concreteComparison: The train leaves Ulaanbaatar at $9{:}45$ and reaches Darkhan at $11{:}20$. How long is the ride? Don't subtract the clock faces — CLIMB: $9{:}45$ to $10{:}00$ is $15$ minutes, to $11{:}00$ is an hour more, to $11{:}20$ is twenty more. Total: $1$ h $35$ min. The cashier's counting-up move from Topic 2, reading a clock.
lessons.objective: Find elapsed time by counting up through round hours, find end times from a start and a duration, and read simple timetables.
concept: **Count up through round hours.** From $9{:}45$: climb $15$ min to $10{:}00$, then whole hours, then the loose minutes — $15 + 60 + 20 = 95$ min $= 1$ h $35$ min. The round hours are the landmarks; the climb is the answer.

**Clock subtraction is a trap.** $11{:}20 - 9{:}45$ column-style hits '$20 - 45$' and tempts a base-ten borrow — but an hour breaks into SIXTY minutes, not a hundred. Counting up avoids the broken borrow entirely.

**End times add the same way.** Start $8{:}40$, duration $1$ h $50$ min: add the hour ($9{:}40$), then the minutes — $40 + 50 = 90$ min $= 1$ h $30$, so $10{:}30$. Minutes past sixty trade up into an hour, always.
lessons.keyIdea: Elapsed time is a climb through round hours — count up to the next hour, across the whole hours, then the loose minutes. Minutes trade at sixty, never at a hundred.

facts.title: The climb
facts.explanation: 15 + 60 + 20 = 95 min = 1 h 35 min — landmarks at the round hours.

facts.title: Minutes trade at sixty
facts.explanation: Past sixty, minutes carry into the hour — never at a hundred.

workedExamples.statement: A train leaves at $9{:}45$ and arrives at $11{:}20$. How long is the journey?
A lesson starts at $8{:}40$ and lasts $1$ h $50$ min. When does it end?
workedExamples.note: Hours first, then minutes — trading at sixty.
workedExamples.solution: Add the hour: $9{:}40$. Add $50$ min: $40 + 50 = 90$ min $= 1$ h $30$ min — trade up: $10{:}30$.

commonMistakes.text: Subtracting clock readings like base-ten numbers — 11:20 − 9:45 with a hundred-borrow.
commonMistakes.correction: An hour breaks into 60 minutes, not 100. Count UP through the round hours instead — the climb never borrows wrong.

commonMistakes.text: Leaving 90 minutes unconverted in an end time — "9:90".
commonMistakes.correction: Sixty minutes make the next hour: 9:90 trades to 10:30. No clock reading carries minutes ≥ 60.

steps.title: Climb, don't subtract
beats: Elapsed time is a journey between clock readings — and the fastest route climbs through the ROUND HOURS.
$9{:}45 \to 11{:}20$: fifteen to the hour, sixty across, twenty beyond — $95$ min $= 1$ h $35$.
Column subtraction on clock faces invites a base-ten borrow into a base-sixty world; the climb never breaks an hour wrong.

steps.title: Climbing the clock
steps.intro: To the hour, across the hours, past the hour.

steps.title: The broken borrow
steps.prompt: Computing $11{:}20 - 9{:}45$ by columns, a student borrows and writes "$1{:}75$". The real elapsed time is:
options: $1$ h $35$ min — the borrowed hour is $60$ min, not $100$
steps.explanation: The borrow crossed an HOUR: $20 + 60 = 80$, then $80 - 45 = 35$ — giving $1$ h $35$. The climb ($15 + 60 + 20 = 95$ min) gets there without any borrow at all.

steps.title: The 24-hour clock skips the guesswork
steps.body: Timetables use $16{:}35$ instead of "4:35 in the afternoon" so that no journey ever looks like it ends before it starts. Reading both clocks — $16{:}35$ IS $4{:}35$ pm — is a five-second skill worth having before every train you'll ever catch.

steps.title: End times and timetables
beats: Start $+$ duration: add hours first, then minutes — and minutes past sixty trade UP: $8{:}40 + 1$ h $50$ → $9{:}40$, then $40 + 50 = 90 = 60 + 30$ → $10{:}30$.
Backwards works too: to arrive at $11{:}00$ after a $35$-min walk, leave by $10{:}25$.
A timetable is rows of this arithmetic: departure, duration, arrival — one of them always missing, the other two rebuilding it.

steps.intro: Hours, then minutes; trade at sixty.

lessons.title: Measurement Word Problems
lessons.concreteComparison: A shelf plan calls for a board of $1.2$ m plus a ledge of $45$ cm. Add them as written — $1.2 + 45 = 46.2$ — and you've built nonsense: metres and centimetres cannot meet in one sum. CONVERT FIRST: $120 + 45 = 165$ cm. Every measurement problem starts with one question — are all my numbers speaking the same unit?
lessons.objective: Solve multi-step measurement problems across length, mass, capacity and time, converting to a common unit BEFORE any arithmetic, and reporting answers in sensible units.
concept: **Convert first.** Mixed units in one computation is the cardinal sin: $1.2$ m $+ 45$ cm becomes $120 + 45 = 165$ cm (or $1.2 + 0.45 = 1.65$ m — either unit works, as long as it's ONE unit).

**Then it's Topics 2 and 3.** Once units agree, measurement problems are event queues, receipts, and division with remainders wearing unit names: a $2$ L bottle minus $750$ ml is $2\,000 - 750 = 1\,250$ ml.
**Answer in a sensible unit.** $3\,600$ g is truthful, but the shopper hears $3.6$ kg. Finish by climbing the ladder to the unit the situation speaks — that last conversion is part of the answer.
lessons.keyIdea: One unit before any arithmetic, familiar arithmetic in the middle, and a sensible unit at the end — the three-part shape of every measurement problem.

facts.title: The three-part shape
facts.explanation: Unit alignment first, Topics 2–3 in the middle, a ladder-climb to finish.

facts.title: The cardinal sin
facts.explanation: Mixed units in one sum build nonsense — 165 cm is the truth.

workedExamples.statement: A board of $1.2$ m and a ledge of $45$ cm are joined end to end. How long is the whole, in centimetres and in metres?
workedExamples.note: Convert first — either unit, but one unit.
workedExamples.solution: Convert: $1.2$ m $= 120$ cm. Add: $120 + 45 = 165$ cm $= 1.65$ m. (Adding $1.2 + 45$ raw would claim a $46$-metre shelf.)

workedExamples.statement: Three parcels each weigh $1$ kg $200$ g. What is the total mass, in a sensible unit?
workedExamples.solution: Each: $1\,200$ g. Total: $3 \times 1\,200 = 3\,600$ g — reported sensibly, $3.6$ kg.

commonMistakes.text: Computing across mixed units — 2 L − 750 ml = 1.25 by luck, or 748 by disaster.
commonMistakes.correction: Convert first, every time: 2,000 − 750 = 1,250 ml. Getting it right by accident once teaches the habit of getting it wrong forever.

commonMistakes.text: Reporting raw ladder-bottom answers — "the parcels weigh 3,600 g".
commonMistakes.correction: True but tone-deaf: climb to the unit the situation speaks — 3.6 kg. The final conversion is part of the answer.

tryIt.statement: A $2$ L kettle is filled from a jug holding $750$ ml, poured twice. How much more water is needed?
A hike covers $3.4$ km before lunch and $2\,800$ m after. What is the day's total, in kilometres?

steps.title: Convert first — the one commandment
beats: Before ANY arithmetic, ask: do all my numbers speak the same unit? $1.2$ m $+ 45$ cm — not yet. Convert: $120 + 45 = 165$ cm.
Either direction works ($1.20 + 0.45 = 1.65$ m) — the sin is mixing, not the choice of unit.
After conversion it's old arithmetic: event queues, receipts, remainders — Topics 2 and 3 wearing unit names.

steps.title: Catch the sin
steps.prompt: A student computes a fence as $2$ m $+ 75$ cm $= 77$ cm... wait — $2 + 75 = 77$. The mistake:
options: metres and centimetres met in one sum — convert first: $200 + 75 = 275$ cm
steps.explanation: The $2$ was METRES: $200$ cm. Aligned, the fence is $275$ cm $= 2.75$ m — three and a half times the broken answer.

steps.title: A spacecraft died of mixed units
steps.body: In 1999 NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter burned up because one team computed thrust in metric units and another in imperial — nobody converted first. The cardinal sin of this lesson, at a cost of $327$ million dollars. Your fence arithmetic and their orbit arithmetic fail the same way.

steps.title: Multi-step, and the sensible finish
beats: Real problems chain steps: convert, run the event queue, then CLIMB BACK to a sensible unit. Three parcels of $1$ kg $200$ g: $3 \times 1\,200 = 3\,600$ g — reported as $3.6$ kg.
Division joins in: a $3$ m ribbon into $40$ cm pieces — $300 \div 40 = 7$ r $20$: seven pieces, $20$ cm left.
The guardrail travels too: estimate in round units ($3$ parcels ≈ $1$ kg each ≈ $3.6$... about $3$–$4$ kg ✓) and the exact answer must land beside it.

steps.title: Sensible reporting
steps.prompt: A hiking day totals $6\,200$ m. The trail sign should say:
steps.explanation: All but the last are true — but kilometres are how trails speak: $6.2$ km. Climbing to the audience's unit is part of the answer.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Convert FIRST — mixed units must never meet in one computation.
The middle is familiar: queues, receipts, remainders — with unit names on.
Finish on the ladder rung the situation speaks (3,600 g → 3.6 kg).
Estimates in round units still guard every answer.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each problem write the one unit you'll work in BEFORE reading the numbers again — the choice, made early, is the whole battle.

steps.title: You've finished "Measurement & Units" — the whole topic
steps.body: Four ladders, one commandment, and a spacecraft's worth of motivation. Two topics remain in Grade 5: shapes and their measurements, then data — both of which will use every unit in this one.

practice.statement: Convert $4$ m $7$ cm to centimetres, and $6\,020$ m to kilometres-and-metres.
Which is longer: $3.05$ m or $340$ cm? By how much?
practice.solution: $3.05$ m $= 305$ cm $< 340$ cm — the $340$ cm ribbon wins by $35$ cm.

practice.statement: Express $7$ kg $80$ g in grams, and $5\,600$ ml in litres.
How many $125$ ml cups does a $1$ L carton fill?
Convert $2\frac{1}{2}$ h to minutes and $400$ s to minutes-and-seconds.
A class runs $9{:}35$ to $11{:}10$. How long is it?
A recipe mixes $1.2$ kg of flour with $300$ g of sugar. Total dry mass, sensibly?
A $4$ m plank is cut into $65$ cm shelves. How many shelves, and what offcut remains?
practice.solution: $400 \div 65 = 6$ r $10$: six shelves and a $10$ cm offcut. Receipt: $6 \times 65 + 10 = 400$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: Convert $8$ km $45$ m to metres, and $2\,930$ cm to metres as a decimal.
Order from lightest to heaviest: $0.9$ kg, $850$ g, $1.05$ kg.
How many $250$ ml bottles fill a $3.5$ L container, and is anything left over?
testYourself.solution: $3\,500 \div 250 = 14$ exactly — fourteen bottles, nothing over. Receipt: $14 \times 250 = 3\,500$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: Convert $1\frac{3}{4}$ h to minutes, and explain why $1.75$ h is NOT $175$ min.
testYourself.solution: $1\frac{3}{4}$ h $= 60 + 45 = 105$ min. The fraction multiplies SIXTY ($\frac{3}{4} \times 60 = 45$), not a hundred — $175$ is the base-ten reflex on a base-sixty ladder.
